name: Chest binding tape

card.summary: Adhesive tape sold for flattening the chest, used by trans men, nonbinary people, performers and others to create a flatter, more masculine or smoother chest line under clothing.
card.note: Health guidance describes tape, elastic bandages and duct tape as linked to breathing, musculoskeletal and skin problems; commercial binders are the option community groups most often name as safer.

quick.overview:
Chest binding tape is adhesive tape applied across the chest to compress breast tissue so the chest looks flatter under clothes. People who bind include transgender men and nonbinary people, who often describe it as easing gender dysphoria and giving a sense of gender euphoria, as well as cisgender men with gynecomastia, drag performers and cosplayers. Tape is one of several methods alongside purpose-made binders and compression sports bras.

Research on binding generally is limited. A 2017 survey of transgender adults found that most reported some physical effect, with the greatest harms linked to improvised materials such as elastic bandages, plastic wrap and duct tape. Some retailers market tape made specifically for binding.
quick.how: Tape is applied directly to the skin of the chest in strips and removed after a period of wear; some users choose it over a binder for hot weather, swimming or because binders are uncomfortable. Products differ in stretch and adhesive, and some are marketed for multi-day wear. Community and clinical guidance describes tape differently from garment binders, so anyone considering it is usually advised to talk to a clinician.
quick.risks: Health guidance and Wikipedia's summary of the literature associate binding with back and chest pain, shortness of breath, skin irritation and tearing from adhesive, and, rarely, rib injury. Duct tape and elastic bandages are described as dangerous or unsafe. Frequency of binding (days per week) has been associated with more complications than hours per session.

lead: Chest binding tape is tape used to flatten the chest by holding breast tissue against the body. It is one of several chest-binding methods, which also include commercial binders, high-compression sports bras, layered clothing and household materials [1].

People bind to look flatter in clothing. Wikipedia's overview lists transgender men and nonbinary people, often to ease gender dysphoria and feel gender euphoria, cisgender men with gynecomastia, drag performers and cosplayers, and people recovering from surgery [1]. Binding has older roots in the moxiong and dudou of China, Japanese sarashi wraps and 1920s flapper fashion [1].

Tape is among the less-studied methods. Duct tape and elastic bandages have been linked to more reported harms than sports bras in survey research, and sources on tape are mainly community surveys and clinical guides [1].

angle.text: While worn, tape compresses the chest so shirts hang flatter. Users also describe the mood benefit of seeing a flatter chest, which is why binding is discussed in both appearance and gender-affirmation contexts.

paras: Wikipedia groups binding methods into commercial binders, high-compression sports bras and athletic tape, and household materials such as elastic bandages, duct tape and plastic wrap [1]. It reports that community organisations generally consider properly sized commercial binders the safest option and describe duct tape and ACE bandages as unsafe [1]. It also notes an unverified claim that some tape made specifically for binding does not compress the ribs or lungs and can be worn for several days [1].

Binding of any kind can cause musculoskeletal pain, shortness of breath, skin irritation and rashes, with rib fractures rare; unsafe binding may cause lasting breast deformation or scarring and, as stated in an overview, long-term binding may affect later mastectomy outcomes [1]. Medical guidance cited by Wikipedia links binding, body and athletic tape to breathing difficulty, musculoskeletal damage and skin damage, and says removing duct tape can hurt or tear skin [1].

A 2017 cross-sectional survey of transgender adults reported that about half had back pain, overheating, chest pain or shortness of breath, and about three in four had skin or tissue effects; elastic bandages, plastic wrap and duct tape were linked to many harms, and days bound per week was more strongly associated with complications than hours per session [1].

Tape is discussed in style and gender-presentation communities as a lightweight alternative when a binder is too hot or bulky, and guidance there stresses limiting wear time and following instructions from clinicians and community health groups [1].

No studies found on tape specifically. A related 2017 cross-sectional survey of transgender adults examined chest binding in general and reported harms associated with different materials, including duct tape and elastic bandages [1].
